title: The Divine Office
hook: monks stop whatever they're doing to pray at set hours, day and night

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Taizé chants, one short line sung until it sinks in. Your line was sing it again. Did a tune keep going under your breath while you worked? Day one thousand three hundred seventy-nine.

Deep in the night, a bell rings in a monastery. Doors open along a dark corridor. Men in robes walk to the church, some still blinking, and begin to sing psalms. A few hours later, at first light, the bell again. Early morning, again. Midmorning. Midday. Midafternoon. Sunset. And once more before sleep. A brother could be kneading bread, or halfway through a sentence in a book, or up a ladder fixing a gutter. When the bell rings, he stops. The day isn't organized around meals or work or meetings. It's organized around prayer, and everything else fits into the gaps. Today's word is the name for that pattern.
screen: `A BELL IN THE NIGHT.` → `AGAIN, AND AGAIN, ALL DAY.` → `EVERYTHING ELSE FITS IN THE GAPS.`

segments.voice: The Divine Office is the round of prayer at set hours, made mostly of psalms, that Christian monks, and others too, keep through the day and night. Here's where it comes from, four ways. First, a verse. The Psalms already speak of praying by the clock: "Seven times a day do I praise thee because of thy righteous judgments." And another line: "At midnight I will rise to give thanks unto thee." Second, a rule. Benedict of Nursia wrote a short rule for monks that is still followed in monasteries today. He takes those two verses at their word. Seven times in the day, he sets an hour of prayer, and once in the night, the night office. In his rule, all the psalms are sung through each week. Third, the bell. Benedict is strict about one thing. When the signal for prayer sounds, he says, a monk should put down whatever is in his hands and come at once, though calmly, without rushing about. He calls the prayer the work of God, and says nothing is to be put before it. Fourth, beyond the monastery. Different churches keep the hours in their own way. Catholics call it the Liturgy of the Hours, and priests, religious and lay people pray it. Anglicans pray Morning and Evening Prayer from the Book of Common Prayer. Orthodox Christians keep their own cycle of hours. Look back over this week: a scene stepped into, a castle, a dark night, one sacred word, shared silence, a sung line. Each was a way to pray. The Office is a way to keep praying, by giving the day a skeleton and hanging everything else on it.
screen: `A VERSE: SEVEN TIMES A DAY.` · `A RULE: BENEDICT SETS THE HOURS.` · `THE BELL: PUT IT DOWN AND COME.` · `BEYOND THE MONASTERY.` · then, large: `SEVEN TIMES A DAY DO I PRAISE THEE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pause at three set hours. First, choose them now. Maybe waking, midday and bedtime. Or before three meals. Then treat this very sit as the first one. Put down whatever is in your hands, literally, and let them rest. If you pray, you can say a line from a psalm you know. If not, breathe and notice the hour: the light in the room, the sounds, what this part of the day is like. Then make a plan to stop again, twice more, for one minute each. The bell holds the time.
The Divine Office. The round of psalms and prayers kept at set hours of the day and night, which Benedict called the work of God. Today's word.

Your line: the hours. Today, when each of your three hours comes, stop, even mid-sentence, the way a monk would at the bell, and take one minute before you pick it back up. Day one thousand three hundred seventy-nine.

howItsDone: Monks and nuns gather in church at set hours to sing psalms and prayers; Catholics also pray the Liturgy of the Hours from a breviary or app, and Anglicans pray Morning and Evening Prayer from the Book of Common Prayer.

notes: Rule of Benedict is paraphrased. Confirm: ch. 16 builds seven day hours and the night office on Psalm 119:164 and 119:62; ch. 18 has the whole psalter sung each week; ch. 43 says to leave whatever is in hand at the signal and hasten, yet with gravity, and that nothing is to be put before the work of God.

'Still followed in monasteries today' and the descriptions of Catholic (Liturgy of the Hours; priests, religious and many lay people), Anglican (Morning and Evening Prayer, BCP) and Orthodox practice are general; confirm wording.
The hook's timetable (night, first light, midmorning, midday, midafternoon, sunset, before sleep) follows Benedict's hours loosely and is illustrative; actual times vary by community.
Editor: the hook listed only six daytime bells while the teach says Benedict sets seven day hours; 'early morning' (Prime) added so the hook's count matches the Rule.
